patient.name: Priya Raman
patient.setting: GP surgery, then the breast clinic
patient.complaint: A painless lump in her left breast, found in the shower 3 weeks ago
background: Combined oral contraceptive pill for 4 years
No family history of breast or ovarian cancer

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' for a young woman with a firm, smooth, **highly mobile** painless lump, against fibrocystic change, cyst, fat necrosis and cancer.

points: Priya, 23, felt a lump in her **left breast** in the shower.
**Painless**; no nipple discharge, no skin change.
Size has **not changed** across her last period.
Feels well: no weight loss, no fever.

steps.lead: A **young, nulliparous** woman is exactly who gets fibroadenomas.

points: Examination: 2 cm lump, **upper outer quadrant**, left breast.
**Firm, smooth, well-defined**; slips away under the fingers.
Not fixed to skin or chest wall; no skin tethering.
No axillary nodes; right breast normal.

steps.lead: That slippery, **highly mobile** lump is the classic **'breast mouse'**. Painless and steady through the cycle fits too.
So the leading diagnosis is a **benign**, hormone-driven tumour of **fibrous and glandular** tissue, with no systemic illness.

steps.q: Which single feature most supports fibroadenoma over cancer in Priya?
o: Lump in the upper outer quadrant
steps.r: Cancer is also often painless and upper outer. **Mobility and a smooth edge** point to fibroadenoma.

visual.title: Lump size across the menstrual cycle
visual.caption: Fibroadenomas do not fluctuate with the cycle; fibrocystic lumps swell and hurt before a period.

steps.lead: Priya's lump is smooth and mobile with no skin change. An **irregular, fixed** lump would need urgent assessment, not reassurance.

steps.text: 'Painless' does not mean benign: breast cancer is usually painless too. Use **mobility, edge and fixation**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'most appropriate initial investigation' (**ultrasound** in young women), 'diagnostic' (**core needle biopsy**), or which referral pathway by age.

steps.q: Priya is 23 with no family history. Which referral does she need?
steps.r: Under 30 with no high-risk family history: **routine** referral. Over 30 would be **2-week-wait**.

visual.title: Age and referral pathway for a new breast lump
visual.label: Priya 23
visual.caption: Thirty is the cut-off. High familial risk makes any age urgent.

steps.lead: Priya is **under 30** with no first-degree relative affected, so **routine** referral is right.

steps.title: Triple assessment at the breast clinic
nodes: 3. Pathology: core needle biopsy if any doubt
All three concordant benign → diagnosis secure
steps.caption: Each limb alone can miss cancer; together they are reliable.

steps.lead: Priya has all three limbs available. At 23 her breasts are dense, so **ultrasound** is the imaging of choice.
Imaging and examination agree, so no doubt remains. Had the ultrasound been **indeterminate**, Priya would need a **core needle biopsy**.
If biopsy were done, **histology** is the gold standard: fibrous stroma and glandular epithelium, no malignancy.

steps.text: Fine needle aspiration is not the answer for a solid lump: **core needle biopsy** gives tissue architecture.

management.exam: Expect 'most appropriate management': reassurance for a typical lump under 3 cm, excision if over 3 cm or growing.

visual.title: Fibroadenoma size and plan
visual.label: Priya 2.1 cm
visual.caption: 3 cm is the number the exam tests.

steps.q: Priya's lump is 2.1 cm, typical on exam and ultrasound. What next?
steps.r: Typical, small (**<3 cm**), no red flags: **reassurance**. Most fibroadenomas are stable or shrink.

steps.lead: Priya is **reassured**: her lump is typical, **under 3 cm**, with no red flags. She is told to return if it grows.
If her lump had any **atypical** feature, a **core needle biopsy** would confirm the histology before any decision.
Two years later, if it grew to 4 cm or bothered her, she would be offered **surgical excision**.

steps.title: Fibroadenoma management
nodes: Typical, <3 cm, no red flags → reassure
>3 cm, symptomatic or growing → surgical excision

steps.lead: Priya's routine referral follows **NICE NG12**: 2-week-wait is for women **30 and over** with an unexplained lump.

steps.text: Exam pairs: **<3 cm typical → reassure; >3 cm or growing → excise**. Uncertain → core biopsy first.
Do not pick 'surgical excision' for every lump: a small, typical fibroadenoma is left alone.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: hormonal drive (oestrogen, progesterone), why it is mobile, why it grows in pregnancy.

steps.title: Why a fibroadenoma forms
nodes: Oestrogen and progesterone act on a lobule
Hyperplastic response of a single lobule
Proliferation of glandular epithelium and fibrous stroma

steps.lead: Priya's lump is one **lobule** overgrowing in response to **oestrogen and progesterone**.
That is why it can **enlarge in pregnancy** or on her pill, and why fibroadenomas **regress after menopause**.
Priya has never been pregnant, so more cycles of **unopposed cyclical oestrogen**.
The lump is **encapsulated**, so it slides under the fingers. Cancer **invades** and fixes to skin or chest wall.
Even with a textbook 'breast mouse', Priya still got **triple assessment**: no single limb reliably rules out cancer.

steps.q: Why does a fibroadenoma move so freely on examination?
o: It is attached to a duct
It is well encapsulated and not fixed to surrounding tissue
It lies within the pectoral fascia
steps.r: A **capsule** separates it from surrounding tissue; malignancy invades and tethers.

steps.text: Hormone link: grows in **pregnancy**, lactation and with oestrogen; shrinks after **menopause**.

mcq.q: Classic description of a fibroadenoma on examination?
Which group is most likely to have a fibroadenoma?
Which feature suggests malignancy rather than fibroadenoma?
o: Irregular, fixed lump with skin changes
mcq.r: Fixed, irregular and skin changes need **urgent assessment**.

mcq.q: Key imaging for a breast lump in a 24 year old?
Gold-standard diagnostic test if imaging is uncertain?
Referral for a new breast lump in a 35 year old woman?
Typical 2 cm fibroadenoma, no red flags. Management?
Size above which fibroadenoma excision is usually offered?

mcq.r: A hyperplastic lobular response to **oestrogen and progesterone**.

mcq.q: Why is a fibroadenoma so mobile?
o: It is attached to the nipple
mcq.r: Not fixed to tissue, skin or chest wall.

technique.stem: A 22 year old woman has noticed a lump in her right breast for 6 weeks. It is painless and does not change in size during her menstrual cycle. There is a 2 cm firm, smooth, well-defined mass in the upper outer quadrant that moves easily under the fingers. There is no skin change or axillary lymphadenopathy.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis. Breast lump questions turn on age and how the lump feels.

clues: does not change in size during her menstrual cycle
steps.x: Young age, painless, no cyclical change, firm smooth and mobile.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A 'breast mouse' in a young woman: **fibroadenoma**.

elim: Cysts are fluctuant and typical in the 40s.
Follows trauma and is often firm, irregular and tethered.
Lumpy and tender, varying with the cycle.

steps.x: **C. Fibroadenoma.** Rule: young + firm + smooth + highly mobile = fibroadenoma.

Poor sensitivity in dense young breasts.
Reserved for specific problems such as high-risk screening.

steps.x: **A. Breast ultrasound.** Rule: young or dense breasts → ultrasound.

technique.stem: A 27 year old woman with a known 2 cm fibroadenoma is now 24 weeks pregnant. She notices the lump has grown to 3 cm. There are no other new features.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism for the increase in size?
o: Raised oestrogen and progesterone stimulating the lobule

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism. Link the timing of the change to hormones.
Growth during pregnancy in a hormone-sensitive tumour.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fibroadenomas respond to **oestrogen and progesterone**.

elim: Growth in pregnancy is expected hormonal behaviour; malignant change is very rare.
That would be a galactocele, not a solid fibroadenoma.
Duct dilatation is duct ectasia, not fibroadenoma growth.
Not the usual explanation for steady growth.

steps.x: **E. Raised oestrogen and progesterone stimulating the lobule.** Rule: hormone-driven, so grows in pregnancy and regresses after menopause.

A hard, irregular mass tethered to skin

o: Loss of oestrogen and progesterone after menopause

prompts.q: What is a fibroadenoma and who gets it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: age and parity in the stem.

points.p: Benign tumour of fibrous and glandular tissue
points.why: Most common benign breast tumour in young women.

points.p: Hormone-driven, no systemic illness
Young women; more common if nulliparous

prompts.q: Describe the classic fibroadenoma on examination.

points.p: Painless, firm, smooth, well-defined
points.why: Painless is not enough to call it benign.

points.p: Highly mobile: 'breast mouse'
Often upper outer quadrant
Does not change with the menstrual cycle

prompts.q: Which features make you think breast cancer rather than fibroadenoma?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: fixed and irregular means urgent.

points.p: Irregular, hard lump
Fixed to skin or chest wall
Skin changes (tethering, peau d'orange)

prompts.q: How do you tell fibroadenoma from fibrocystic change and a cyst?

points.p: Fibrocystic: lumpy, tender, swells before periods
Cyst: smooth, fluctuant, older women

prompts.q: What is triple assessment, and which imaging suits a young woman?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: every new lump gets all three.

points.p: Clinical examination
Imaging: ultrasound in young/dense breasts, mammogram may be used
Biopsy if needed: core needle biopsy

prompts.q: Which referral pathway applies to a new breast lump, and what family history makes it urgent?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the age of 30 is the line.

points.p: Over 30: urgent 2-week-wait
Under 30: routine referral
First-degree male relative any age, or relative under 40
Bilateral cancer under 50, or two first-degree relatives

prompts.q: How is a fibroadenoma managed? Give the size cut-off.

points.p: Typical, <3 cm, no red flags: reassurance
Atypical: core needle biopsy first
>3 cm, symptomatic or growing: surgical excision

prompts.q: Why does a fibroadenoma form and why is it hormone-sensitive?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one lobule, two hormones.

points.p: Hyperplastic response of a single lobule
points.why: Glandular epithelium and fibrous stroma both proliferate.

points.p: Driven by oestrogen and progesterone
points.why: Unopposed cyclical oestrogen explains nulliparity link.

points.p: Enlarges in pregnancy or with oestrogen; regresses after menopause
points.why: Growth in pregnancy is not malignant change.

prompts.q: Why is a fibroadenoma mobile, and why is triple assessment still needed?

points.p: Well encapsulated, not fixed to tissue, skin or chest wall
Neither exam nor imaging alone is reliably discriminatory

glossary.Fibroadenoma: A benign breast tumour of fibrous and glandular tissue, common in young women.
glossary.Breast mouse: Nickname for a fibroadenoma because it slips away under the fingers.
glossary.Parous: Having given birth at least once.
glossary.Benign: Not cancerous; does not invade or spread.
glossary.Stroma: The supporting connective tissue of an organ.
glossary.Glandular epithelium: The lining cells of the breast ducts and lobules.
glossary.Lobule: A milk-producing unit of the breast.
glossary.Hyperplastic: Showing an increased number of normal cells.
glossary.Encapsulated: Surrounded by a capsule that separates it from neighbouring tissue.
glossary.Triple assessment: Clinical examination, imaging and biopsy together for every new breast lump.
glossary.Core needle biopsy: A wide needle removes a core of tissue for histology.
glossary.Fine needle aspiration: A thin needle takes cells or fluid for cytology; less informative than a core.
glossary.Histology: Study of tissue structure under the microscope.
glossary.2-week-wait: Urgent NHS suspected-cancer referral: seen within two weeks.
glossary.NICE NG12: NICE guideline on recognising and referring suspected cancer.
glossary.Upper outer quadrant: The part of the breast towards the armpit; holds most breast tissue.
glossary.Fibrocystic change: Benign lumpiness and tenderness that varies with the menstrual cycle.
glossary.Breast cyst: A fluid-filled sac in the breast, common in women in their 40s.
glossary.Fat necrosis: Damaged fat forming a firm lump, usually after trauma or surgery.
glossary.Phyllodes tumour: A rare, fast-growing fibroepithelial tumour that can be benign or malignant.
glossary.Intraductal papilloma: A benign growth in a duct that typically causes bloody nipple discharge.
glossary.Skin tethering: Skin pulled in by an underlying lump, a sign of malignancy.
glossary.Peau d'orange: Dimpled orange-peel skin from lymphatic blockage by tumour.
glossary.Anechoic: Black on ultrasound; contains clear fluid.
glossary.Unopposed oestrogen: Oestrogen action without the balancing effect of progesterone.
glossary.Menopause: The end of menstruation, confirmed after 12 months without periods.
glossary.Mammogram: Low-dose breast X-ray; less useful in dense young breasts.
glossary.Concordant: All three parts of triple assessment agree.
glossary.Galactocele: A milk-filled cyst in a breastfeeding woman.
glossary.Duct ectasia: Dilated ducts behind the nipple in older women, causing discharge.
